script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Good morning, and welcome to the Eastside Public Library. How can I help you today?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Good morning. I'd like to become a member, please. I want a card so I can borrow books and book one of the study rooms.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Of course. The first step is a short registration form. Could I take your surname, please?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: It's Pemberton. That's P, E, M, B, E, R, T, O, N.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Thank you. And your first name?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Daniel.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Could you confirm your date of birth for me?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Yes. It's the fourteenth of March, nineteen ninety-eight.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Lovely. Now I need your current address. Are you still in the flat on Harbour Road?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I am, but I've moved to a different building on the same road. It's number thirty-seven now.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Thirty-seven Harbour Road. Is that right?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That's right.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: And a contact number?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: It's zero four one two, three four five, six seven eight.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Thanks. Now, the fees. Adults pay twenty-five pounds a year. Full-time students pay half that rate, but you'll need to show a valid student card.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I'm a full-time student at the university, so I'll bring my card. What's the student rate exactly?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: It's twelve pounds fifty for the year. That covers everything except fines for late returns.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Fair enough. How long does the membership last?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: One year from the day you join. You can borrow up to eight items at a time.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Eight. And how long can I keep them?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Standard loans run for three weeks. You can renew each item twice, provided nobody else has reserved it.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Can I renew online?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Yes, online or by phone. Just have your card number ready.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Good. What do I need to prove my address?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: A recent utility bill or a bank statement with your name and new address on it. Your student card covers your identity.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I've got a gas bill in my bag. Will that do?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Perfect, as long as it's dated within the last three months.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Great. Also, are the study rooms bookable at weekends?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: They are. We're open from nine until five on Saturdays, and rooms can be booked for up to two hours at a time.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Two hours. That should be enough for my group project.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Let me print your card details. Please sign here, and I'll take your photograph for the card.

title: Guided tour of Riverside Botanic Garden

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Riverside Botanic Garden. I'm Ruth, and I'll be guiding you around for the next hour.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: The tour begins at the north gate, next to the car park. If you arrived by bus, you'll need to walk about five minutes uphill to reach it.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Before we set off, a few practical points. The café is open from ten in the morning until four in the afternoon. It's the only place on site where you can buy hot food, so plan your lunch around that.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Our most famous feature is the tropical glasshouse. It was built in 1887, and it still houses plants that were brought back by Victorian plant hunters.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Unfortunately, the Herb Garden is closed this month. The team is replacing the irrigation system, and the work should finish by the end of the season.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Photography is welcome throughout the gardens, but please don't use flash inside the glasshouse, because the light can damage some of the older plants.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: You'll notice many of the orchids in the glasshouse are labelled with small cards. Please don't touch them. The oils from our hands can harm the flowers, and some of these orchids are extremely rare.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Guided tours like this one usually last about sixty minutes, and then you're free to explore on your own. We have a lot of benches, so feel free to sit down whenever you need to.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Now, if you hold a Riverside membership card, you can visit free on Tuesdays. Those visits don't need to be booked in advance. Everyone else pays the standard entry fee at the gate.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Finally, please take your litter home with you. We don't have bins in the woodland area, in order to protect the wildlife.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Right, let's go through the plan for your urban bird survey. Priya, you've drafted the sampling sites. Talk us through them.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Sure. We've selected six sites across the city: two parks, two residential streets, and two near the railway line. I chose the railway sites because we expected more species there, but I'm not sure that's the case.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: That's a useful hypothesis to test. Tom, what about timing?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We were going to survey at dawn for one hour, but I'm worried that's too early for some students who don't live nearby. Could we do late morning instead?

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Dawn is standard for bird counts, because most species are most active then. You'd miss a lot of activity later in the day.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Right, I hadn't considered that. So we keep dawn, but we could reduce the survey to forty-five minutes.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Forty-five minutes should be fine if you're consistent. Priya, what about the recording method? Were you planning to note every bird you see?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Actually, I'd prefer to use a point count method: stand still at one spot and record every bird heard or seen within a fixed radius for ten minutes.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Good. That's standard for urban habitats, where you can't walk long transects easily. What radius did you decide on?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Fifty metres. Anything further and it's hard to be sure which bird you're hearing.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Agreed. Tom, you wanted to add a sound-recording device?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Yes, a small recorder left at each site overnight. It would let us check species we might have missed, and we can analyse the recordings later.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Helpful, but it comes with a cost. Do you know what the equipment costs?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: About two hundred and eighty pounds per unit. We have budget for three, so we'd need to rotate them between the six sites.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Then rotate them, and be clear in your report that the overnight data covers fewer sites. Also, don't forget the weather. Surveys shouldn't go ahead in heavy rain or strong wind.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We've put that in the protocol. We'll record the wind speed and temperature at the start of each count.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Excellent. And the final deadline for the report?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: The third of December. We'll need the data processed by mid-November to leave time for writing.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Good. Your next step is to pilot the point-count method at one park this week. Come back to me with the results on Friday.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Today I want to look at terrace farming, one of the oldest methods humans have used to work steep land. You'll find terraces in the Andes, in the Philippines, and in the hills of southern Italy.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: The basic idea is simple. Instead of farming a steep slope as one continuous surface, farmers cut it into a series of flat steps. Each step, or terrace, holds soil and water in place.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: The most important benefit is erosion control. On a bare slope, heavy rain can wash away the topsoil within a few seasons. Terraces slow the water down, so the soil has time to soak in rather than run off.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Terraces also make irrigation easier. Water can be directed across each level, and in many traditional systems it flows down from one terrace to the next. This is far more efficient than trying to water a steep hillside from the top.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: However, building terraces takes enormous effort. The retaining walls are usually built from local stone, and in a typical hillside project a team might need several years to finish a single terrace system.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: That is why maintenance matters so much. A terrace wall that is not repaired after a storm can collapse, and once one wall fails, the water it held can cut through the soil behind it very quickly.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Now let's look at a case study. In a survey of abandoned terraces in a mountain region of Nepal, researchers found that nearly seventy percent of the walls had collapsed within twenty years of the farmers leaving.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: The researchers' main finding was that the loss of terraces was not caused by weather alone. Labour migration to the cities removed the people who used to repair the walls every year.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: This matters for policy. Some governments now offer grants to help farmers repair terraces before they fail, rather than paying for emergency work afterwards. Those programmes have proved cheaper in the long run.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Let's turn to crop choice. On terraces, farmers traditionally grow crops with shallow roots, such as beans and potatoes, because deep roots can disturb the retaining walls.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: A final point concerns water. Many terrace systems were designed around seasonal rain, so they store water in small ponds at the top of each slope. Modern engineers often copy this approach when they plan drainage for new housing estates.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: For your assignment, I'd like you to compare two sites: one that still has working terraces and one where they have been abandoned. Use the evidence from the case study, and note the specific factor that explains the difference.
